one_sentence: The Brain observes and records everything your organization does, before trying to understand any of it.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Nothing your organization does goes unrecorded — the first step toward never losing knowledge again.
one_sentence_variants.product: Every meeting, email, and message a user touches becomes a raw signal the Brain can later surface back to them.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: A passive ingestion layer with no interpretation logic — it collects raw activity and preserves source information.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: Think of it as the Brain's eyes and ears — it just watches, it doesn't judge anything yet.

why_it_exists: If the Brain doesn't observe an event, it never existed as far as the organization's memory is concerned. Without a dedicated capture step, every other layer would be reasoning over gaps and guesses instead of what actually happened.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Every meeting, email, and decision your company makes is currently invisible to any system. Capture is what stops that knowledge from evaporating the moment the conversation ends.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without capture, none of the context you want to show a user later would exist — there'd be nothing to surface inside Gmail, Slack, or the CRM.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Skipping capture means Understanding has to work from incomplete, unsourced signals — provenance breaks at the very first step.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Imagine if your company simply forgot every meeting the moment it ended. Capture is the layer that stops that from happening.

what_it_does: Capture ingests raw organizational signals — calendar events, meeting transcripts, emails, Slack messages, CRM notes, documents, workflow events — and preserves them with their source and timestamp. It does not interpret meaning yet; that is the Understanding layer's job. Its only responsibility is making sure nothing gets missed.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It quietly collects everything happening across your tools — meetings, emails, messages — so nothing important is ever lost to time or turnover.
what_it_does_variants.product: It hooks into the tools your users already use (Gmail, Slack, Calendar, CRM) and pulls in raw activity the moment it happens, with zero extra effort from the user.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: people, meetings, emails, chats, systems, documents, workflows, events. Outputs: raw activity, raw events, raw communications, raw organizational signals — source-tagged and timestamped, uninterpreted.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the layer that notices things happened — a meeting, an email, a Slack message — and writes them down before anyone has figured out what they mean.

real_example: A team meeting happens on Zoom. An email thread about a client is exchanged. A Slack message assigns a task to someone. A contract document is uploaded to a shared drive. All of these are captured as raw signals — audio, text, documents, system events — before any interpretation occurs. None of it is understood yet; it's simply preserved as the raw material for the Understanding layer.
technical_depth: Capture is the first of the Company Brain's seven core layers (Capture → Understand → Memory → Intelligence → Execution → Exposure → Evolution). Its responsibilities are strictly: collect organizational signals, preserve source information, record activity. Inputs are unstructured: people, meetings, emails, chats, systems, documents, workflows, events. Outputs are raw activity, raw events, raw communications, raw organizational signals — none of it yet decomposed into Atomic Primitives. That decomposition is explicitly the Understanding layer's responsibility, not Capture's.

one_sentence: The Brain reads everything it captured and works out what it actually means in terms of how the organization works.

one_sentence_variants.executive: This is where raw activity turns into something your organization can actually use — structured understanding, not just a transcript.
one_sentence_variants.product: This is the step where a meeting transcript becomes 'Sarah promised X to Acme by Friday' instead of just a wall of text.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Decomposes captured activity into the ten Atomic Primitives and emits Canonical Knowledge Objects.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: Think of it as the Brain's reading comprehension — it figures out who did what, who promised what, and why it matters.

why_it_exists: Raw activity by itself is just noise — a transcript, an email thread, a Slack log. Without a step that extracts who was involved, what was promised, and what changed, the Brain would have lots of data and zero understanding.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: A pile of meeting recordings isn't knowledge. Understanding is what turns activity your company already generates into something it can actually act on.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this step, there's nothing structured to ever show a user — no commitment to flag, no risk to surface, just unparsed text.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Memory cannot consume unstructured signals — it requires Canonical Knowledge Objects. Understanding is the only layer that produces them.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: If nobody ever made sense of what happened in a meeting, the Brain would just be a pile of recordings — not actually useful to anyone.

what_it_does: Understanding reads captured activity and identifies the ten Atomic Primitives present in it — who was involved (Actor), what was said (Communication), what was promised (Commitment), what was done (Action), and so on. It then packages these into Canonical Knowledge Objects, the Brain's standardized representation format, ready to be stored as memory.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It reads every conversation and interaction and pulls out what actually matters: who's accountable, what was promised, what's at stake.
what_it_does_variants.product: It turns 'we talked about the proposal on the call' into a structured record your product can actually query and surface later.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Identifies Actors, Communications, Commitments, Actions, Resources, Rules, Goals, Relationships present in captured signals; produces Canonical Knowledge Objects as output, consumed by the Memory layer.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's like a really good notetaker who doesn't just write down what was said, but also tags who promised what and what it means for the team.

real_example: From the Zoom meeting captured earlier, Understanding reads the transcript and identifies: Sarah (Actor) made a commitment (Commitment primitive) to deliver the client proposal (Resource) to Acme Corp (Actor) by Friday (Time). It packages this as a Commitment Object — structured, typed, and traceable to the meeting where it was made.
technical_depth: Understanding's responsibilities: identify the atomic primitives present in every signal (Actors, Communications, Commitments, Actions, Resources, Rules, Goals, Relationships), transform captured activity into structured organizational understanding, and produce Canonical Knowledge Objects representing organizational reality. Inputs: captured organizational activity. Outputs: structured organizational reality represented as Canonical Knowledge Objects — the representation layer consumed by Memory, Intelligence, and external systems.

one_sentence: Before the Brain can remember anything, it needs a standard way to write things down — that standard format is a Knowledge Object.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Knowledge Objects are the consistent format that makes everything the Brain learns traceable, auditable, and portable.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the structured version of 'Sarah promised the Acme proposal by Friday' that your product can actually display, link, and search.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The canonical representation layer between Understanding and Memory: human-readable, AI-readable, traceable, versionable, portable.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: Think of it like the index card a librarian fills out before filing a book — title, author, subject. That card is the Knowledge Object.

why_it_exists: Memory needs a standardized input format to stay consistent and queryable across everything the Brain has ever learned. Without a canonical representation, every memory record would be shaped differently and nothing could be reliably compared, linked, or audited.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Consistency is what makes the Brain auditable. Knowledge Objects are why every piece of memory can be traced back to its source, no matter when it was created.
why_it_exists_variants.product: If every captured event were stored in a different shape, nothing in your product could reliably query or display it consistently.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Memory Formation requires a normalized input — without Knowledge Objects, Memory would need bespoke ingestion logic per source type, breaking provenance and versioning guarantees.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Imagine if every person at your company kept notes in a totally different format — nobody could ever find anything. Knowledge Objects make sure everyone (and every AI) writes things down the same way.

what_it_does: Knowledge Objects are canonical representations of organizational reality produced by the Understanding layer. They are not memory themselves — they are the representation layer from which memory is formed. Primitive Knowledge Objects map one-to-one to the eight storable Atomic Primitives (Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, Relationship). Composite Knowledge Objects (Person, Team, Meeting, Policy) are built by combining primitive ones, mirroring how the Ontology composes higher-order concepts.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's the Brain's standardized paperwork — every fact, promise, and action gets written down the same consistent way, so nothing is ever ambiguous or untraceable.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the structured data shape behind every card, chip, and context panel your product ever shows a user.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Eight Primitive Knowledge Object types (Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, Relationship Object) form a closed set, owned by Architecture & Vision. Composite Knowledge Objects (Person, Team, Meeting, Policy Object, etc.) are owned by the Ontology and built by combining primitives.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's version of a standardized form — no matter who or what filled it out, it always has the same fields in the same place.

real_example: A sales call happens. The Brain creates a Person Object for each participant, a Meeting Object for the call itself, and a Commitment Object for the Q3 proposal promise. Each one follows the exact same structural rules — human-readable, AI-readable, traceable back to the original meeting — regardless of who said what or which tool the meeting happened in.
technical_depth: Two-tier model: Primitive Knowledge Objects (Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, Relationship Object — a closed, fixed set of eight, owned by Architecture & Vision v2.2 §9) and Composite Knowledge Objects (Person, Team, Project, Policy, Workflow, Meeting, Initiative Object, etc., owned by the Ontology, built by combining primitives per Ontology §3). Commitment exists in both tiers intentionally — as a Primitive Knowledge Object representing the primitive, and as a Composite Knowledge Object representing the ontology object. Knowledge Objects must be human-readable, AI-readable, traceable, versionable, portable, and governed. They are not memory — Memory Formation consumes them but they are not persisted as Knowledge Objects themselves.

one_sentence: The Brain stores everything the organization knows, organized into five types of knowledge that each decay and get queried differently.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Think of it as your organization's long-term memory — structured, governed, and queryable at any time, by anyone with the right authority.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why a user can ask 'what did we promise this client?' six months later and actually get a real answer.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Five distinct memory stores with defined inputs, outputs, lifecycle rules, and write governance, consuming Canonical Knowledge Objects.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: Imagine if every meeting, promise, and lesson learned was automatically filed in the right place and never forgotten. That's Memory.

why_it_exists: Organizations forget constantly. Without structured memory, every meeting ends and the knowledge disappears, decisions get repeated, context is lost, and AI agents work blind.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Every organization already has this problem — knowledge walks out the door with whoever leaves. Memory is the fix.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without persistent memory, every feature that depends on 'remembering' a user's history would have nothing to draw from.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Knowledge Objects are transient representations — without a persistence layer with provenance and lifecycle rules, nothing the Understanding layer produces would survive past the current session.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: You've probably seen someone ask 'why did we decide this?' and nobody remembers. Memory exists so that never has to happen again.

what_it_does: The Memory Layer receives Knowledge Objects from Understanding and routes them into five purpose-built memory stores, each optimized for a different kind of organizational knowledge. Every record carries provenance: who said it, when, from what source, and with what confidence. Nothing is anonymous, and nothing can be silently changed.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It files everything the Brain learns into the right kind of long-term record — facts, reasoning, promises, actions, and lessons — each governed and sourced.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the backend that lets your product answer 'what happened, who said it, and when' for anything a user has ever done inside your tools.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Routes Knowledge Objects into Factual, Interaction, Commitment, Action, and Learning Memory based on Memory Formation routing rules. A single event may write to multiple stores simultaneously, sharing a common source reference while remaining independently queryable.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's like five different filing cabinets, each one built for a different kind of thing your company needs to remember.

real_example: A sales call happens. The Brain routes the meeting record to Interaction Memory (why it happened), the verbal Q3 commitment to Commitment Memory (who owes what), and the Acme Corp account update to Factual Memory (what exists). Three months later, when a new account manager takes over, all three are still there — complete, sourced, and connected.
technical_depth: Memory Layer operates on Canonical Knowledge Objects produced by the Understanding Layer. Responsibilities: maintain five distinct memory stores, attach provenance/time/state to every record, preserve relationships and links across memory types, track the lifecycle of every open commitment, serve relevant memory to Intelligence on demand. Write governance: humans may create Factual, Interaction, Commitment, and Learning memory subject to authority; AI may propose updates requiring automatic, delegated, or human approval; automation is restricted to predefined scopes. Conflicts are never silently overwritten — both versions persist, one Current, one Superseded.

one_sentence: Memory stores things; Intelligence reads across all of it and figures out what it means — risks, opportunities, and what to do next.

one_sentence_variants.executive: This is the layer that turns stored knowledge into actual foresight — risks flagged before they happen, not after.
one_sentence_variants.product: This is what generates the suggestion a user sees, not just the data behind it.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Reasons over all five memory stores to generate ten types of intelligence objects, each carrying confidence, sources, and a reasoning trace.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: If Memory is the Brain's filing cabinet, Intelligence is the part that actually reads the files and notices patterns a person might miss.

why_it_exists: Stored knowledge has no operational value on its own. Without a layer that reasons over memory, nobody would ever notice that a commitment is overdue, a risk is forming, or an opportunity is closing — until it was too late.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Data sitting in a database doesn't prevent anything. Intelligence is what catches the renewal at risk before it's lost, not after the client leaves.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this layer, your product would just be a searchable archive — useful for lookup, but never proactive.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Memory has no operational value without a consumer that reasons over it. Without Intelligence, every memory record is just inert storage.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Imagine having a perfect memory but never connecting any of the dots. Intelligence is the part of the Brain that connects them.

what_it_does: Intelligence reads across Factual, Interaction, Commitment, Action, and Learning Memory, assembles relevant context, and reasons over it to generate ten types of outputs: Recommendations, Operational Risks, Opportunity Signals, Drift Signals, Knowledge Gaps, Predictions, Policy Violations, Process Bottlenecks, Agent Readiness assessments, and Brain Scores. Every output carries a confidence level and is never presented as certainty.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It continuously scans everything the organization knows and surfaces what actually needs attention — risks, opportunities, and recommended next steps.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the reasoning engine behind every risk badge, recommendation card, or 'you should know this' moment your product can ever show.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Reasoning pipeline: Context → Situation Understanding → Goal Evaluation → Constraint Evaluation → Commitment Evaluation → Risk Evaluation → Opportunity Evaluation → Recommendation Generation. Behavior branches by Consultant mode (Inquiry, Planning, Review, Simulation). Every output is an Intelligence Object with Sources, Confidence, Timestamp, Owner, and Review Trigger.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the part of the Brain that notices things like 'hey, this promise is 30 days overdue and nobody's followed up' — without anyone having to ask.

real_example: Intelligence reads Commitment Memory and notices that Sarah's proposal commitment is now 2 days past the Friday deadline with no status update recorded in Action Memory. It cross-references Factual Memory and finds the Acme account is linked to a $200k Q3 revenue target. Operational Risk generated: 'Commitment at risk of breach — no progress recorded, deadline passed. Confidence: High.'
technical_depth: Intelligence consumes all five memory stores plus current actor, goal, query, constraints, and environment. Context Assembly weighs relevance, recency, goal linkage, actor proximity, commitment linkage, and explicit references into a bounded Context Package. Confidence Model has five levels (Very Low → Very High) with asymmetric handling: Operational Risk and Drift Signal are never withheld at low confidence (tracked with an 'unconfirmed' flag), while Recommendations and Agent actions are withheld below threshold. Adaptive Intelligence learns only from Repeated Validated Feedback — never from a single instance — and writes back to memory only through Memory Model's existing Write Governance.

one_sentence: This is where intelligence becomes action — humans and AI agents actually doing the work, informed by everything the Brain knows.

one_sentence_variants.executive: This is where insight turns into outcomes — work actually gets done, informed rather than guessed at.
one_sentence_variants.product: This is the layer where a user (or an agent acting on their behalf) actually completes the task the Brain flagged.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Transforms Intelligence and Recommendations into actions and outcomes, performed by humans, AI agents, workflows, or automations.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just people and AI doing the actual work — but now they're not guessing, because the Brain already told them what matters.

why_it_exists: Recommendations and risk flags are worthless if nothing ever happens because of them. Execution exists to close the loop between knowing something and acting on it.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Insight without action is just a report nobody reads. Execution is what makes the Brain's intelligence actually change outcomes.
why_it_exists_variants.product: If there's no execution step, every smart suggestion the Brain generates just sits there unactioned.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without a defined Execution layer, Recommendations and Agent Readiness assessments would have no consumer — the reasoning pipeline would terminate without effect.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: The Brain can tell you what to do all day long — Execution is the part where it actually gets done.

what_it_does: Execution is where humans and AI agents complete commitments, run workflows, coordinate activity, and operate the organization — informed by Intelligence's recommendations rather than acting blind. Every action taken here gets recorded back into Memory, closing the loop: execution creates new reality, which becomes new memory, which generates new intelligence.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's the actual work getting done — but now backed by full context instead of guesswork, and every action feeds back into what the Brain knows.
what_it_does_variants.product: This is the 'Assign to Agent' button, the task getting completed, the email actually getting sent — and the Brain logging that it happened.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Participants: humans (employees, managers, operators, executives) and AI (assistants, agents, workflows, automations). Every action produces an Action Memory record, closing the Capture → Understand → Memory → Intelligence → Execution loop.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's just the doing part — sending the email, finishing the task, making the call — except now informed by everything the Brain already knows.

real_example: Sarah's manager Maria receives the Operational Risk alert about the overdue Acme proposal. She schedules a check-in call with Sarah — a human action, recorded in Action Memory. A Brain agent automatically drafts a follow-up email to the client acknowledging the delay — an agent action, also recorded. Both actions update the commitment status and feed new learning signals into Evolution.
technical_depth: Inputs: Intelligence and recommendations. Outputs: actions and outcomes, written to Action Memory. Execution does not replace human or AI judgment — it operationalizes Intelligence output by giving humans and agents the context to act correctly. Agent execution is additionally gated by Agent Readiness (Intelligence Architecture) and Agent Authority (Trust & Governance) — both axes must pass before an agent acts autonomously.

one_sentence: The Brain delivers memory and intelligence to the right person, at the right moment, through the tool they're already using — without anyone having to ask.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Your team doesn't have to go looking for answers — the Brain brings the answer to them, inside the tools they already use.
one_sentence_variants.product: This is the layer responsible for the actual panel, suggestion, or context card a user sees inside Gmail, Slack, or your product.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Delivers Memory, Intelligence, and Execution outputs via Ambient Delivery, Agent Access, or Mission Control, governed by the same provenance and trust as every other layer.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the part of the Brain that hands you exactly what you need, right when you need it — instead of making you go dig for it.

why_it_exists: Memory and intelligence only have value once they reach the point of work. Without a delivery layer, the Brain would know everything and tell no one — useful knowledge would still require someone to manually go search for it.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: The smartest insight in the world is worthless if nobody sees it in time. Exposure is why your team finds out before the client does.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without Exposure, the Brain would just be a backend database — none of the 'it just showed up when I needed it' moments would exist.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Memory and Intelligence have no path to the point of work without a dedicated delivery layer — Principle 8 (Right Memory, Right Moment) requires Exposure as a first-class architectural responsibility, not an afterthought.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Knowing something doesn't help if you never tell anyone. Exposure is the Brain actually telling people — at the right time.

what_it_does: Exposure delivers memory, intelligence, and actions to humans and AI through Ambient Delivery (inside Gmail, Slack, Calendar, CRM), Agent Access (MCP responses to AI tools), and Mission Control (dedicated investigation views). It decides who needs to know something, where it should appear, when, and how — and stays silent when there's nothing useful to say.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It decides who needs to see what, and pushes it to them automatically — no dashboards to check, no searching required.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the integration layer: Gmail panels, Slack suggestions, calendar briefs, CRM context cards, MCP responses to AI agents.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Responsibilities: Ambient Delivery, Agent Access, Mission Control Delivery, Reality Feed Distribution, Context Injection, Notification Routing, Multi-channel Memory Exposure. Outputs include Slack Suggestions, Email Context, Calendar Briefs, CRM Context, MCP Responses, Reality Feed Items.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the part of the Brain that taps you on the shoulder with exactly the right info, right when you're about to need it.

real_example: Maria opens Gmail to write to the Acme client about Sarah's delayed proposal. The Brain's Gmail integration surfaces inside the compose window — without Maria switching tabs: full Acme commitment history, the risk flag, Sarah's last recorded status. Maria writes a more informed email in 2 minutes instead of spending 15 minutes hunting through Slack and the CRM.
technical_depth: Inputs: Memory, Intelligence, Execution. Key questions: who needs to know this, where should it appear, when, how should it be delivered. Outputs: Slack Suggestions, Email Context, Calendar Briefs, CRM Context, Browser Extension Context, MCP Responses, Reality Feed Items, Mission Control Views. Design rule (Product Architecture §4): the Brain never interrupts, never forces interaction, and remains silent when no useful memory exists. Every suggestion is contextual, dismissible, explainable, and traceable.

one_sentence: The Brain doesn't just remember — every time a recommendation succeeds, fails, or gets ignored, it learns from that outcome too.

one_sentence_variants.executive: This is what makes the Brain get smarter about your specific organization over time, not just more capable in general.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why the same suggestion that gets dismissed three times in a row eventually stops appearing, or starts appearing differently.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Closes the organizational learning loop: evaluates outcomes, compares designed processes against executed Action patterns, and proposes validated learning back to Memory through standard Write Governance.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain noticing 'hey, that thing I suggested last time actually worked' — and getting a little better at suggesting it next time.

why_it_exists: An organization that doesn't learn from its own outcomes is doomed to repeat the same failures. Without Evolution, every recommendation accepted or rejected, every risk that resolved or escalated, would be a one-time event with no lasting effect on how the Brain reasons in the future.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: The same mistake happening three times, in three different teams, is a failure of organizational memory — Evolution is what stops that pattern.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product's recommendations would never improve based on how real users actually responded to them.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without a feedback mechanism, Adaptive Intelligence (Intelligence Architecture Part 14) would have no write path, and the reasoning pipeline would never improve from its own track record.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: This is why institutional knowledge matters — and why it shouldn't only live in people's heads. Evolution makes sure the Brain actually remembers what worked.

what_it_does: Evolution evaluates outcomes — accepted suggestions, rejected suggestions, agent successes and failures, exposure effectiveness — and asks what the Brain should learn from them. It also compares designed processes (Policy, SOP) against what Action Memory shows actually happened, surfacing confirmed process drift as candidate improvements. Crucially, a single piece of feedback never becomes learning by itself — only patterns validated across multiple independent instances do, and even then the proposed learning must pass through Memory's normal Write Governance before it's written.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It tracks what worked and what didn't across the whole organization, and turns validated patterns into permanent improvements — reviewed by a human before they take effect.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the layer that notices a feature suggestion gets accepted 9 times out of 10 in one context but rejected in another, and adjusts.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Actions, outcomes, feedback signals, recommendation outcomes, exposure outcomes. Learning Rule: Observation ≠ Learning, Single Feedback ≠ Learning, Repeated Validated Feedback = Learning. Validated learning is proposed as a Learning Memory candidate and requires approval per Memory Model's Write Governance — Intelligence proposes, Memory governs the write.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the part of the Brain that says 'this has now happened three separate times — there's probably a real lesson here' instead of overreacting to one bad day.

real_example: After tracking 10 similar client proposal commitments over 6 months, Evolution detects a pattern: 'Proposal commitments without a recorded pricing approval are 4x more likely to be delayed.' It proposes this as a candidate learning record. After the pattern recurs independently across multiple teams, it is approved and written to Learning Memory — and every future proposal commitment without pricing approval is immediately flagged.
technical_depth: Inputs: actions, outcomes, feedback signals, recommendation outcomes, exposure outcomes (accepted/rejected/ignored suggestions, agent approval/rejection rates, exposure effectiveness). Outputs: updated organizational memory, updated understanding, updated learning signals, policy improvement candidates. The Adaptive Boundary (Intelligence Architecture Part 14) is explicit: the Brain may improve reasoning, but may not silently rewrite organizational memory — every write-back passes through Memory Model v1.2 §9's standard Write Governance.

one_sentence: An Actor is anything that can participate in organizational activity — a person, a team, a customer, a vendor, or an AI agent.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every person, team, customer, vendor, or AI agent your company deals with is tracked as an Actor — so accountability is never ambiguous.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's how the Brain knows the difference between 'the user', 'their manager', and 'the customer they're emailing' in any given context.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The first of ten Atomic Primitives — the foundation every Commitment, Communication, and Action ultimately references.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It just means 'who's involved' — could be a person, a whole team, a customer, or even an AI.

why_it_exists: Every other primitive either involves Actors or exists to serve them — Commitments are between Actors, Communications happen between Actors. Without Actors, organizational reality has no participants and no accountability.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Without a consistent concept of 'who', accountability falls apart — you can't track who owes what if 'who' isn't well-defined.
why_it_exists_variants.product: If the Brain didn't model AI agents as Actors too, there'd be no consistent way to show 'an agent did this' the same way it shows 'a person did this'.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Commitment and Communication primitives are both defined relative to Actors — without this primitive, the other nine have nothing to attach to.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: If the Brain couldn't tell people, teams, and customers apart, it could never answer 'who promised this?'

what_it_does: An Actor is intentionally broad: anything that can make commitments, take actions, communicate, or be held accountable is an Actor — including AI agents, treated as first-class participants rather than tools.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It treats every participant — human or AI — as someone who can be held accountable, with a name and a track record.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the entity behind every avatar, every 'assigned to', every 'sent by' your product shows.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Actor Object (Primitive Knowledge Object) and to Person/Team/Customer/Vendor/Agent (Composite Knowledge Objects, Ontology Layer 2).
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a deliberately wide net — a person, a department, a customer, even a compliance bot, all count as Actors.

real_example: Sarah (individual employee), the Enterprise Sales Team, Acme Corp (external customer), the Legal Department, a compliance AI agent running automated checks — all are Actors. The Brain tracks who is accountable for what by treating every participant, human or AI, as a first-class Actor.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-001 (Actor Object), a Primitive Knowledge Object. Primary memory home: Factual Memory, referenced as a participant by every Interaction, Commitment, and Action record (Memory Model v1.2 §10). Composite Knowledge Objects built from Actor include Person, Team, Customer, Vendor, Agent (Ontology Layer 2).

one_sentence: A Communication is any exchange of meaning between Actors — meetings, emails, messages, requests, discussions.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every meeting, email, and message is treated as a single consistent type — meaning nothing communicated is structurally invisible to the Brain.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the raw material behind every 'previous conversation' context your product can ever surface.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The primitive from which Commitments and reconstructed Decisions are derived.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It just means anything where information passed between people — a Slack message, an email, a meeting.

why_it_exists: Communications are the raw material from which Commitments are born and Decisions are made. Without treating every exchange as the same underlying primitive, the Brain couldn't reliably extract the promises and reasoning hidden inside them.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Most commitments and decisions start as a sentence in a meeting or email — Communication is what lets the Brain catch that sentence.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, there's no consistent place for 'where did this commitment come from' to point back to.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Decision (a Layer 4 ontology composite) is built from Communication + Goal + Rule + Commitment — without this primitive, Decision has no source material to reconstruct from.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's how the Brain notices that a throwaway line in a meeting ('I'll handle that') was actually a promise.

what_it_does: A Communication carries intent, information, decisions, requests, or feedback from one Actor to another. The Brain captures Communications not just as records of what was said, but as the source from which hidden Commitments, implicit Goals, or contested Rules get identified.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's how every conversation your team has gets scanned for the promises and decisions hidden inside it.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the structured form behind 'show me what was discussed' anywhere in your product.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Communication Object (Primitive Knowledge Object); primary memory home is Interaction Memory, the source of new Commitments and the basis for reconstructing Decisions.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It covers everything from a quick Slack message to a full client meeting — anything where meaning passed between people.

real_example: A Slack message: 'Can you handle the Acme proposal by Thursday?' is a Communication that contains a latent Commitment request. The reply 'Yes, I'll have it done' is a Communication that creates a Commitment. The Brain treats every one of these as the same primitive type because they all carry meaning between Actors.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-002 (Communication Object). Primary memory home: Interaction Memory (Memory Model v1.2 §10). Decision (Ontology Layer 4) is reconstructed from Communication + Goal + Rule + Commitment, not stored as its own object.

one_sentence: A Commitment is any obligation between Actors — a promise, a task assignment, an expectation, or an authorization to act.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every promise made anywhere in your company is tracked as a living record with a real status — not a note someone might remember.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the data behind every 'overdue' badge or 'you promised this' reminder your product can show.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: One of the most critical primitives — the only one with a fully governed eight-state lifecycle.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's a promise — 'I'll send the proposal by Friday' — tracked from the moment it's made until it's kept or broken.

why_it_exists: Most organizational failure happens when commitments are unclear, forgotten, duplicated, or not tracked across their full lifecycle. Without this primitive, 'who owes what to whom' would live only in people's memory.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Broken commitments erode trust faster than almost any other organizational failure — this primitive exists to make sure none silently disappear.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, there'd be no reliable way to ever show a user 'this is still outstanding.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Commitment Memory's entire purpose depends on this primitive carrying explicit state — without it, 'overdue' or 'breached' couldn't be computed at all.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Ever had someone forget something they promised in a meeting? This primitive exists so the Brain never does that.

what_it_does: The Brain treats every Commitment as a living record with an explicit state, not a static note, so it can always answer who owes what to whom and what the current status is. It moves through an eight-state lifecycle: Requested → Promised → one of Fulfilled, Declined, Delegated, Cancelled, Renegotiated, or Breached.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It tracks every promise from the moment it's made through to fulfilled, broken, or reassigned — automatically, without a status meeting.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the lifecycle state machine behind any 'task' or 'promise' feature — Requested, Promised, Fulfilled, Breached, and more.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Eight-state lifecycle: Requested → Promised → Fulfilled / Declined / Delegated / Cancelled / Renegotiated / Breached. Delegated and Renegotiated always link forward to a new commitment record rather than mutating the original.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's not just 'a note from the meeting' — the Brain actively tracks it until it's done, broken, or handed off to someone else.

real_example: Sarah says in a meeting: 'I'll send the proposal to Acme by Friday.' That creates a Commitment: Actor = Sarah, deliverable = Acme proposal, due = Friday. When Friday passes without a delivery recorded in Action Memory, the Brain automatically updates the Commitment state to Breached and generates an Operational Risk alert.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-003 (Commitment Object) — notably the only primitive that is also a first-class Composite Knowledge Object/ontology object (Ontology v1.2 §3). Per-subtype lifecycle restrictions exist (e.g. Customer Promise disallows Delegated) — absence from that table means the full eight-state lifecycle applies. Primary memory home: Commitment Memory.

one_sentence: An Action is work performed that actually changes something — closing the gap between what was promised and what really happened.

one_sentence_variants.executive: This is how the Brain tells the difference between what was promised and what was actually delivered.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the record created the moment a task is actually completed, not just assigned.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The primitive that fulfills or breaches Commitments, and the ground truth source for drift detection against SOPs.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: If Commitment is the promise, Action is the proof it actually happened.

why_it_exists: The gap between intended reality (a Commitment) and actual reality (an Action) is where most organizational risk and learning live. Without tracking Actions separately from Commitments, the Brain couldn't tell a kept promise from a broken one.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Knowing what was promised isn't enough — Action is what proves whether it actually happened.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, there'd be no way to mark a task 'done' versus just 'assigned.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Drift detection (comparing SOP against Workflow) depends entirely on Action Memory as ground truth — without Action as a distinct primitive, there's no observed reality to compare against intended reality.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the difference between someone saying they'll do something and them actually doing it.

what_it_does: An Action is work performed that changes organizational state — a process executed, a file delivered, a workflow completed, an incident resolved. Actions close Commitments and produce outcomes, and every Action is recorded with who did it and when.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It records exactly what got done, by whom, and when — turning promises into a verifiable track record.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the event that flips a commitment from 'open' to 'fulfilled' in your product's UI.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Action Object (Primitive Knowledge Object); written to Action Memory; updates Resource state and fulfills or breaches open Commitments.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's literally just 'this got done' — sending the email, finishing the report, resolving the ticket.

real_example: Sarah sends the proposal email. That is an Action: it creates a record in Action Memory linking back to the original Commitment, marking it Fulfilled, timestamping when it happened. If instead she updated the deadline (Renegotiated) or handed it to a colleague (Delegated), those would also be Actions.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-004 (Action Object). Primary memory home: Action Memory. Per Memory Model v1.2 §11, Action's resulting state change is not reified into a separate object — Action Memory already carries the before/after state, which Pattern Detection reads directly.

one_sentence: A Resource is anything that can be used, consumed, managed, or affected — money, documents, accounts, systems, time.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how the Brain tracks what's actually at stake or being used in any commitment or action — budget, documents, accounts.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the 'what' behind 'deliver this document' or 'spend this budget' that your product needs to track.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: What Commitments concern and what Actions act upon — critical for detecting capacity conflicts across competing commitments.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just 'the thing being worked on' — a document, a budget, a shared resource like a meeting room.

why_it_exists: Understanding which Resources are involved in any activity is key to understanding organizational risk, capacity, and dependency — especially when multiple Commitments compete for the same Resource.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Without tracking Resources, the Brain couldn't flag that two high-priority commitments are quietly competing for the same person's time.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, there's no way to show 'this is blocked because the same resource is tied up elsewhere.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Capacity-risk detection in Intelligence depends on Resource as a distinct primitive — otherwise contention between competing Commitments is invisible.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why the Brain can notice 'these two promises both need the same engineer's time' before it becomes a problem.

what_it_does: Resources are what Commitments concern ('I will deliver this document') and what Actions act upon ('the document was delivered'). The Brain tracks Resources to detect contention — when multiple Commitments depend on the same limited Resource.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It tracks the budgets, documents, and shared assets your commitments actually depend on.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the object reference behind 'this deliverable' or 'this budget line' anywhere a commitment touches something concrete.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Resource Object (Primitive Knowledge Object); referenced by Action (what was acted on) and Commitment (what was promised).
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the actual 'thing' involved — the document, the money, the meeting room, the dataset.

real_example: The Acme proposal document Sarah is creating is a Resource. The $50k budget that needs CFO approval is a Resource. When the Brain detects that two high-priority Commitments both depend on the same engineer's time, it can proactively flag a capacity Risk before either commitment falls behind.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-005 (Resource Object). Primary memory home: Factual Memory, referenced by Action and Commitment records rather than stored independently per use.

one_sentence: A Rule is any constraint, policy, authority structure, or governing principle — what defines what is and isn't allowed.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how every approval threshold and spending limit your company has is something the Brain can actually check against.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the thing your product checks before letting an action proceed without review.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: What Intelligence compares actual Actions against to detect drift and Policy Violations.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just 'the rule' — like 'deals over $100k need VP approval.'

why_it_exists: Rules define who can approve what and what the organization has formally decided about how it should operate. Without this primitive, the Brain would have no governing principle to check actual behavior against.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Without Rules as a distinct concept, there'd be nothing for the Brain to catch a policy violation against.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, 'requires approval' would just be a label with no actual enforcement logic behind it.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Policy Violation and Drift Signal detection both depend on Rule as the comparison baseline against Action Memory — without it, there's no 'intended' side of the comparison.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the written-down version of 'this is how we're supposed to do things here.'

what_it_does: A Rule defines approval thresholds, security policies, escalation paths, spending limits, hiring protocols, and compliance requirements. When Action Memory shows behavior that doesn't match a Rule, the Brain detects the gap automatically — before anyone has to manually audit the paper trail.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's every spending limit, approval threshold, and compliance requirement your company has — now checkable automatically.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the policy your feature enforces — 'requires manager approval', 'cannot exceed $X' — made checkable, not just written down.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Rule Object (Primitive Knowledge Object); primary memory home is Factual Memory, referenced by Commitment (terms and authority) and Intelligence (compliance checks).
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the formal version of 'we're not allowed to do that without sign-off.'

real_example: A policy stating 'all client proposals above $100k require VP approval before sending' is a Rule stored in Factual Memory. When Action Memory shows a $145k proposal was sent without a VP approval record, the Brain detects the Rule violation and generates a Policy Violation — before anyone has to manually audit the paper trail.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-006 (Rule Object). Primary memory home: Factual Memory, referenced by Commitment (terms and authority) and Intelligence (compliance checks).

one_sentence: A Goal is a desired future state — it gives meaning and direction to commitments, resources, and rules.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how the Brain knows which risks and opportunities actually matter — relative to what your company is trying to achieve.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the 'why this matters' context behind any recommendation your product surfaces.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The lens through which Intelligence evaluates relevance and urgency of every other output.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just 'what we're trying to accomplish' — like 'grow revenue 20% this quarter.'

why_it_exists: A risk only matters in the context of a goal it threatens; an opportunity only matters if there's a goal it serves. Without Goals, the Brain would have facts and promises with no sense of why any of them matter.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Risk and opportunity are meaningless in a vacuum — Goal is what tells the Brain whether something actually threatens what your company cares about.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, every recommendation your product shows would lack the 'so what' that makes it worth a user's attention.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Intelligence's relevance scoring during Context Assembly is anchored to active Goals — without this primitive, prioritization between competing signals has no basis.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It explains the 'why' behind everything else — why a promise matters, why a risk is worth worrying about.

what_it_does: Goals explain why specific Commitments were made, why particular Resources are being used, why certain Rules exist. The Brain frames every Recommendation in the context of an active Goal, so intelligence outputs are never floating advice disconnected from what actually matters.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's the strategic target every recommendation gets measured against — so nothing surfaces without a clear 'why it matters.'
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the context line your product can show alongside a recommendation: 'this matters because of X goal.'
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Goal Object (Primitive Knowledge Object); primary memory home is Factual Memory, referenced by Interaction (why a decision was made) and Intelligence (progress evaluation).
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the target everyone's working toward — and the reason the Brain thinks something is worth flagging.

real_example: Q3 strategic goal: 'Grow enterprise revenue by 20%.' When the Brain generates a Recommendation, it always frames it in context: 'To achieve the Q3 enterprise revenue target, the Acme renewal is currently at high risk due to 3 unresolved commitments. Recommended action: executive outreach this week.'
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-007 (Goal Object). Primary memory home: Factual Memory, referenced by Interaction Memory (why a decision was made) and Intelligence (progress evaluation). Composite: Goal (Ontology Layer 3, Organizational Structures), built from Goal Primitive + Relationships + Time.

one_sentence: State is the current condition of something — open, in progress, resolved, breached — and it's a property of every record, not a separate store.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how the Brain always knows 'what's currently at risk' without anyone having to ask.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the status badge — open, overdue, resolved — attached to literally everything the Brain tracks.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: A cross-cutting attribute carried by every memory record in every memory type, not a separate store.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just the current status of something — like whether a task is 'done' or 'still open.'

why_it_exists: Without explicit State, the Brain would have to infer whether something is overdue or resolved from context every time, which is unreliable. State makes memory dynamic rather than static.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: If status had to be inferred every time instead of tracked explicitly, 'what's overdue right now' would never have a reliable answer.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without explicit State, your product couldn't reliably render a status badge — it'd have to guess from surrounding text.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without State as a first-class cross-cutting attribute, time-sensitive queries ('what's currently at risk') would require expensive inference rather than a direct field read.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why the Brain can instantly tell you what's still open and what's done, instead of you having to re-read the whole history.

what_it_does: State is never inferred from context — it is explicitly tracked and updated by the Brain as each relevant event occurs, enabling time-sensitive questions like 'what's currently at risk?' and 'what commitments are now overdue?' to be answered directly.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's the explicit status on every record — so 'what's at risk right now' is always a direct answer, not a guess.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the field your UI binds to for every status pill, progress indicator, or 'overdue' flag.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Carried as a field on every record across all five memory types; updated explicitly on each relevant lifecycle transition rather than inferred.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the 'where things stand right now' label that's attached to everything — never something you have to guess at.

real_example: A Commitment moves through states: Requested → Promised → Breached (deadline passed). A customer account state transitions: Active → At Risk → Churned. State is never inferred — it is explicitly tracked, so at any moment the Brain can answer 'what's the current state of every open commitment?'
technical_depth: Cross-cutting attribute on every memory record, not a separate store (Architecture & Vision v2.2 §5; Memory Model v1.2 §10). Every Commitment, Action, and fact carries its current condition as a field rather than as a separate State Change object.

one_sentence: Time is the temporal dimension attached to every organizational event — when it happened, when it's due, how long it's been open.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how the Brain knows something is overdue before a person ever has to check a calendar.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the timestamp behind every 'X days ago' or 'due in 2 days' your product shows.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: A cross-cutting attribute on every record, enabling silence-duration and overdue calculations without a separate reminder system.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just 'when' — when something happened, when it's due, how long it's been sitting there.

why_it_exists: Without Time as an explicit attribute, the Brain couldn't answer time-sensitive questions at scale — what's overdue, what's changed since last Monday, how long has this risk been open.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Nobody should need to set a reminder for the Brain to notice something's overdue — Time is why it doesn't.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, your product couldn't show 'overdue by 3 days' — it would only know 'overdue', with no sense of how badly.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Pre-breach risk detection (e.g. 26 hours until breach) depends on Time being tracked as a queryable attribute, not just a creation timestamp.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why the Brain can say 'this has been sitting for 5 days' instead of just 'this exists.'

what_it_does: Time enables the Brain to answer time-sensitive questions at scale: what's overdue, what's changed recently, how long has this Operational Risk been open without resolution, which commitments have been silent for more than a week.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's what lets the Brain flag a risk before the deadline passes, not after.
what_it_does_variants.product: It powers every relative-time display and overdue calculation in your product, automatically.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Carried as creation timestamp, due timestamp, and last-activity timestamp on every record — enabling silence-duration calculations that drive pre-breach risk alerts.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the clock running quietly behind every promise and task, so nothing just goes silent without anyone noticing.

real_example: A Commitment is made Monday with a Friday deadline. The Brain tracks creation timestamp, due timestamp, and last-activity timestamp. By Thursday 3pm with no activity, it calculates 94 hours of silence and 26 hours until breach, surfacing a pre-breach risk alert automatically — not because someone set a reminder.
technical_depth: Cross-cutting attribute on every memory record, not a separate store (Architecture & Vision v2.2 §5). Drives Intelligence's freshness and decay calculations (Intelligence Architecture v1.0 §15.1).

one_sentence: A Relationship is a meaningful connection between primitives — reports-to, depends-on, caused-by — that turns isolated facts into a navigable model.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's why the Brain can trace a single risk all the way back to the goal, owner, and approval chain it actually affects.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the connective tissue behind 'related commitments' or 'people involved' sections your product can show.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The connective structure across all memory types — not a separate store, but links expressed throughout.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just how things are connected — like 'Sarah reports to Maria' or 'this depends on that.'

why_it_exists: Without Relationships, the Brain holds isolated facts. With them, it can reason about chains and dependencies — turning a collection of facts into a navigable model of how the organization actually works.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Isolated facts don't explain anything — Relationship is what lets the Brain trace cause and effect across your whole organization.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product could show individual facts but never the connected story behind them.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without Relationship as a first-class primitive, traversal queries (who's affected, what depends on what) would require ad hoc joins instead of a consistent graph structure.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's what lets the Brain answer 'who else is involved in this?' instead of just listing facts one at a time.

what_it_does: Relationships connect Actors to Actors, Commitments to Resources, Rules to Authority — letting the Brain traverse the graph to show who's involved, what's at risk, what goals are affected, and whose approval is needed, all from one starting point.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's how a single question — 'what's going on with Acme?' — pulls in everyone and everything actually connected to it.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the graph traversal behind any 'see related' or 'who else is involved' feature.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Maps to the Relationship Object (Primitive Knowledge Object); expressed as links across all memory types rather than stored as an independent record type.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the web of connections the Brain follows to pull together everyone and everything related to one topic.

real_example: Sarah reports-to Maria. Sarah's proposal Commitment depends-on a pricing decision. The pricing decision requires approval from the CFO. When the Brain surfaces context for a meeting about Acme, it traverses these relationships to show who's involved, what's at risk, and whose approval is needed — all from following the relationship graph.
technical_depth: Maps to MAIN-KO-008 (Relationship Object). Not a separate memory store — expressed as links across all memory types, forming the graph structure the Relationship Explorer (Phase 3) will traverse.

one_sentence: Factual Memory is the Brain's organizational directory and policy library — who works here, what teams exist, what's active right now.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the always-current org chart and policy book — except it actually gets used by every other part of the Brain.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the source of truth behind 'who owns this account' or 'what team is this' anywhere in your product.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Stores stable organizational reality: Actors, Resources, Goals, Policies, SOPs, Organizational Structures. Lifecycle: Observed → Recorded → Updated → Superseded → Archived.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the reference layer that answers 'who works here and what's true right now' — the stuff that doesn't change every day.

why_it_exists: Without a reference layer for what currently exists, every other reasoning step would be working from stale or ambiguous facts — like recommending an approval from a manager who already left.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: If your org chart drifts out of sync with reality, every downstream recommendation inherits that error — Factual Memory is what keeps that from happening.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, any feature that depends on 'who owns this' would be working from outdated assumptions.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Every other memory type implicitly depends on Factual Memory staying current — Interaction, Commitment, and Action records all reference Actors and Goals defined here.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why the Brain doesn't keep recommending things to your old manager after they've left the company.

what_it_does: It stores people, teams, departments, roles, goals, policies, SOPs, and resources — the stable layer that every other layer's reasoning builds on. When something here changes (a team restructures, a policy updates), the Brain knows to re-evaluate any intelligence that was built on the previous fact.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's the always-up-to-date map of who's responsible for what across your whole company.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the reference data your product queries for 'who owns this' or 'what's the current policy.'
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Actors, Resources, Goals, Policies, SOPs, Organizational Structures. Typical queries: who owns this, what teams exist, what policy governs this, which role has authority.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the part of memory that just knows the basic facts — who's on what team, what the rules are right now.

real_example: Factual Memory stores: 'Sarah Chen, Senior Account Executive, reports to Maria Lopez, primary owner of Acme Corp account.' When Maria leaves and James takes over, Factual Memory updates — and the Brain automatically reassigns ownership context for all open commitments and risks linked to Maria's authority.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Observed → Recorded → Updated → Superseded → Archived — not every record passes through every stage. Highest-risk memory type for conflicts (Memory Model v1.2 §10), e.g. two systems disagreeing about account ownership. Conflicting facts are never silently overwritten — both persist, one Current, one Superseded.

one_sentence: Interaction Memory preserves organizational reasoning — not just what was decided, but why, and who disagreed.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the institutional memory of why decisions were made — so it doesn't disappear when the people who made them leave.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why a user can ask 'why did we decide this?' and get the actual reasoning, not a guess.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Stores discussion, negotiation, and approval context. Lifecycle: Observed → Interpreted → Recorded → Linked → Archived.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It answers the question every new hire asks: 'why do we do it this way?'

why_it_exists: Without Interaction Memory, organizations lose their institutional reasoning — keeping the outputs of decisions but losing the thinking that produced them, every time someone leaves.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Every time someone with key context leaves, your company normally loses the 'why' behind their decisions — this is what stops that.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, there's no way to ever answer 'why was this built this way?' inside your own product.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Decision (Ontology Layer 4) is reconstructed from Interaction Memory + Commitment Memory + Factual Memory — without this store, half of Decision's reconstruction has no source.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: This is exactly why 'why did we do it this way?' so often goes unanswered — until a Brain actually keeps the reasoning around.

what_it_does: It records not just the decision but the full reasoning: what alternatives were considered, who objected, what the deciding factor was, and who held final authority. This preserves the reasoning behind decisions so it doesn't die with the people who made them.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It keeps the actual reasoning behind big calls on file — alternatives considered, objections raised, who decided.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the structured 'why' your product can surface next to any decision or commitment.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Meetings, Discussions, Negotiations, Approvals, Communications. Typical queries: why was this discussed, what alternatives existed, who objected.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the part of memory that keeps the actual discussion around, not just the final outcome.

real_example: A critical decision: 'We chose Vendor A over Vendor B.' Interaction Memory records the full reasoning: 'Vendor B was cheaper but had two security incidents. Legal and Security both preferred Vendor A. Final authority: CTO.' When a new engineer questions the vendor choice 8 months later, the Brain surfaces the exact reasoning — not a vague summary from memory.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Observed → Interpreted → Recorded → Linked → Archived. A single meeting generates one Interaction record (the discussion and reasoning) and N Commitment records (the obligations it produced) — Memory Model v1.2 §5's worked example.

one_sentence: Commitment Memory tracks every promise across the organization in real time — who owes what, and what's overdue.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's a live, real-time picture of every open promise across your company — no status meeting required.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why your product can show 'this is overdue' without anyone manually flagging it.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Future-oriented memory type — describes intended reality rather than observed reality. Lifecycle: Requested → Promised → Fulfilled/Declined/Delegated/Cancelled/Renegotiated/Breached.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's promise tracker — keeping tabs on everything anyone has committed to, automatically.

why_it_exists: This is what makes the Brain fundamentally different from a document repository or note-taking tool — without it, 'who owes what to whom' requires a search through Slack history instead of a direct answer.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: This is the single highest-leverage store in the whole system — broken promises are the number one driver of client churn that never shows up in your CRM.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product has no reliable way to ever say 'this was promised and it's late.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: The only memory type that is future-oriented by design — most other memory types describe what happened or what exists; this one describes what is supposed to happen.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the reason the Brain can tell you 'hey, this promise is overdue' without anyone having to remember to check.

what_it_does: It tracks every promise, task, responsibility, assignment, and obligation with explicit state, at every moment in its lifecycle. By week 3 of a planning cycle, without anyone asking, it can flag breached, at-risk, renegotiated, and delegated commitments automatically.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It gives a manager a complete picture of every open commitment on their team, without running a status meeting.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the backing store behind every task, promise, or 'assigned to' feature with a real deadline.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Assignments, Requests, Responsibilities, Promises, Decisions (decisions trigger commitments but are themselves reconstructed, not stored). Special property: future-oriented.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain quietly keeping score of every promise made — who said what, and whether they followed through.

real_example: A quarterly planning session generates 34 commitments across 6 teams. By week 3, without anyone asking, Commitment Memory has automatically flagged 5 as Breached, 8 as At Risk, 3 as Renegotiated, and 2 as Delegated. A manager has a complete picture without running a status meeting.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Requested → Promised → one of Fulfilled, Declined, Delegated, Cancelled, Renegotiated, or Breached. Per-subtype restrictions exist (Memory Model v1.2 §6.3): Customer Promise disallows Delegated and requires explicit customer-facing notice for Renegotiated. New subtypes inherit the full 8-state lifecycle unless explicitly restricted.

one_sentence: Action Memory preserves what actually happened — observed reality, not the intended version.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the objective record of how work actually gets done — not how the process document says it should.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why your product can show 'here's what actually happened' instead of just 'here's what was supposed to happen.'
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Represents observed execution reality, used as ground truth for drift detection against Factual Memory's SOPs/Rules.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the record of what really happened — as opposed to what was supposed to happen.

why_it_exists: Without an objective record of execution, the Brain could never tell the difference between how the organization says it works and how it actually works in practice.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Every process document describes the ideal. Action Memory is what tells you what's actually happening on the ground.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, drift between 'designed flow' and 'real usage' would be invisible to your product entirely.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: This is the entire basis for Drift Signal detection — Intelligence compares this store directly against Factual Memory's SOPs/Rules to find divergence.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's how the Brain notices that a process on paper doesn't match what people are actually doing — without anyone running an audit.

what_it_does: It records every process run, incident resolved, workflow completed, and exception handled — creating an objective ground truth that Intelligence continuously compares against intended processes to detect drift.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's the proof of what's really happening across your operations — which is often different from what the policy says should happen.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the execution log behind any 'workflow actually ran like this' feature.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Executions, Workflow runs, Incidents, Exceptions, State changes. Special property: represents observed reality, not intended reality.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's record of what people actually did — which sometimes differs from the official process.

real_example: The standard customer onboarding process has 8 steps defined in Factual Memory. Action Memory, after 60 completed cases, reveals that step 5 (security review) was skipped in 42% of cases — not intentionally, but because the review request goes to a shared inbox that's frequently missed. The Brain detected this pattern without anyone running a manual audit.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Observed → Recorded → Linked → Used → Archived (stages, not a required sequence). Per Ontology v1.2 §3, Workflow is not stored — it is reconstructed on demand from Action Memory's executed steps, Commitment Memory's fulfilled commitments, and Factual Memory's underlying SOP/Rule.

one_sentence: Learning Memory preserves organizational wisdom — validated patterns, lessons, and heuristics — and is the only memory type designed to decay.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's hard-won organizational experience, captured permanently — except, unlike a person, it can't resign and take it with them.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why the same mistake doesn't quietly repeat itself release after release.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Prescriptive rather than descriptive — tells the Brain how to reason more accurately about similar future situations. Subject to decay.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's accumulated experience — the lessons that usually only live in a few people's heads.

why_it_exists: Organizations that don't learn are organizations that can't scale — without Learning Memory, the same mistake happens repeatedly because no one connected this failure to the last one.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Every repeated failure is a failure of organizational memory, not individual competence — Learning Memory exists to stop the repetition.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, the same usability complaint could resurface release after release with nobody noticing the pattern.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Adaptive Intelligence's write path (Intelligence Architecture Part 14) terminates here — validated patterns are proposed as Learning Memory candidates and pass through standard Write Governance before being written.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why 'institutional knowledge' shouldn't only live in people's heads — it gets captured here instead.

what_it_does: It stores lessons, heuristics, patterns, and process improvements discovered through experience — but only after a pattern is validated across multiple independent instances, never from a single occurrence. Confidence in a lesson can decay over time as organizational reality changes.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It captures validated lessons from real outcomes — but only once a pattern repeats, never from a single bad day.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the pattern-detection store behind 'we've seen this before' insights your product can surface.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Outcomes, Patterns, Failures, Successes, Drift Analysis. Special property: the primary memory type subject to decay — lessons lose relevance as organizational reality changes.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's where the Brain keeps the lessons it's learned — but only the ones that have actually proven true more than once.

real_example: After tracking three consecutive product launches that all encountered last-minute legal review delays, Learning Memory records a validated pattern: 'Launches that don't involve Legal from Month 2 onward encounter a 3–6 week delay, confirmed across 3 independent instances.' The next launch planned without early Legal involvement gets flagged immediately — before any delay materializes.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Created → Validated → Used → Reinforced or Decayed → Archived. Decay is distinct from archival — a fully decayed Learning record is not automatically archived and may later be reinforced if the conditions that produced it recur (Memory Model v1.2 §7).

one_sentence: A Recommendation is the Brain's most direct output: here's what you should do, why, and who should act on it.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's a specific, sourced suggestion for action — not a vague insight someone has to interpret.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the suggestion card a user actually sees, complete with reasoning they can inspect.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Draft → Presented → Accepted / Rejected / Modified. Withheld at Low/Very Low confidence by default — acting wrong is costlier than delaying.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain literally telling someone 'you should probably do this, and here's why.'

why_it_exists: Without a concrete recommended action, intelligence is just an observation nobody knows what to do with. Recommendation exists to turn reasoning into something a specific person can actually act on.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: An insight without a next step doesn't change anything — Recommendation is what closes that gap.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, every smart pattern your product detects would have no way of telling a user what to actually do about it.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Recommendation is the terminal stage of the full Reasoning Pipeline (Context → Situation → Goal → Constraint → Commitment → Risk → Opportunity Evaluation) — without it, the pipeline produces analysis with no actionable output.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Knowing something is wrong doesn't help if nobody says what to do about it — that's what a Recommendation is for.

what_it_does: It's the result of the full reasoning pipeline distilled into an actionable suggestion with reasoning and sources attached. Every Recommendation has a named owner, a confidence level, and a lifecycle — it stays open until someone accepts, rejects, or modifies it, and the Brain tracks what happened.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It names exactly who should act, what they should do, and why — with the evidence attached.
