what_it_does_variants.product: It's a structured object: action, reasoning, confidence, sources, owner — everything your UI needs to render a trustworthy suggestion.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Context, Goals, Rules, Commitments, Learning. Outputs: Recommendation, Reasoning, Confidence, Sources. Every recommendation must answer 'why this recommendation?'
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It always comes with the reasoning attached — never just 'do this' with no explanation.

real_example: Acme Corp renewal is in 45 days. Last 3 support tickets are unresolved. Executive sponsor hasn't been engaged in 60 days. Recommendation generated: 'Schedule executive check-in with Acme this week. Renewal at high risk. Owner: Maria Lopez. Confidence: High. Review Trigger: Acme meeting scheduled.'
technical_depth: Owner: typically the actor or team the recommendation is directed at. Confidence asymmetry (Intelligence Architecture Part 13): Recommendations at Low/Very Low confidence are withheld by default, including when confidence decays below threshold while sitting unanswered in Presented state — re-flagged as stale rather than left at original confidence.

one_sentence: An Operational Risk is a detected future threat to goals, commitments, resources, or organizational health — and it's never hidden, even when unconfirmed.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's an early warning — surfaced even before the Brain is fully certain, because missing a real risk costs more than a false alarm.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the alert badge that shows up before a problem actually happens, not after.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Uniquely never withheld at Low/Very Low confidence — tracked with an 'unconfirmed' flag instead, per the Confidence Model's asymmetric handling rule.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain saying 'heads up, this might go wrong' — well before it actually does.

why_it_exists: It is better to flag an unconfirmed risk than to miss a real one. Without this output, threats to goals and commitments would only become visible after they'd already caused damage.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: By the time a risk is obvious to everyone, it's usually too late to act cheaply — this output exists to catch it earlier.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product could only ever react to problems after the fact, never warn ahead of time.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: The asymmetric confidence handling rule (Intelligence Architecture Part 13) exists specifically because under-reporting a possible risk is more costly than a false positive — this is the one output type built around that asymmetry.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the difference between finding out a deadline was missed versus being warned three days before it happens.

what_it_does: It detects possible future threats from open commitments, historical failures, policy violations, resource constraints, and drift signals — and stays open and visible until genuinely resolved, even as its confidence rises or falls over time.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It watches for anything that could threaten a goal or commitment, and flags it early — even while still uncertain.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the risk badge with a confidence level attached, so users know how seriously to treat it.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Sources: Open Commitments, Historical Failures, Policy Violations, Resource Constraints, Drift Signals. Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Tracked → Resolved.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a heads-up about something that could go wrong — flagged early, even if the Brain isn't 100% sure yet.

real_example: Three senior engineers are assigned to the same critical infrastructure release, all near full capacity, with two blocked dependencies. Operational Risk generated: 'Release at capacity and dependency risk. Owner: Engineering Lead James. Confidence: High. Severity: High.' The risk stays open until both blocked items resolve.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Tracked → Resolved. Decay scope: applies only while in active/open states — once Resolved, retains historical confidence permanently, mirroring Memory Model's Archive Path (Intelligence Architecture §15.1).

one_sentence: An Opportunity Signal is the optimistic counterpart to Operational Risk — a chance to create value while the window is still open.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how the Brain catches a chance to gain ground before the window for it closes.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the 'this is worth acting on right now' nudge, based on patterns that have actually worked before.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Pattern-detected hint only — becomes the Layer-4 ontology object Opportunity once resources are formally committed to pursuing it.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain noticing 'hey, this is a good moment to act' instead of just flagging problems.

why_it_exists: Without a dedicated output for positive signals, the Brain would only ever flag problems — opportunities would go unnoticed until the favorable timing window had already closed.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: A system that only flags risk misses half the picture — Opportunity Signal is how upside gets caught too, not just downside.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, your product could warn about problems but never proactively suggest a win.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Sourced from Learning Memory's success patterns specifically — distinguishing it from Risk, which sources from failures and violations.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain being optimistic for once — noticing a good moment instead of just a bad one.

what_it_does: It recognizes patterns in Learning Memory of what has worked before, notices available resources, and detects favorable timing — then surfaces the opportunity while it's still actionable, not after it has passed.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It spots a favorable moment based on what's actually worked in the past, and flags it while there's still time to act.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's a recommendation, but framed around upside — 'act now, here's the historical pattern that supports it.'
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Sources: Success Patterns, Customer Signals, Resource Availability, Relationship Signals, Learning Memory. Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Pursued / Dismissed.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain saying 'this is a great moment to act' — based on patterns that have actually worked before.

real_example: Learning Memory shows: responding to enterprise RFPs within 48 hours triples win rate, confirmed across 14 cases. A high-value RFP just arrived 4 hours ago. Opportunity Signal generated: 'Assign proposal lead immediately. Confidence: High. Review Trigger: 24 hours elapsed.'
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Pursued / Dismissed. Per Ontology v1.2 §7: Opportunity Signal is the Intelligence layer's pattern-detected hint — it only becomes the Layer-4 ontology object Opportunity once a human or agent commits resources to formally pursuing it.

one_sentence: A Drift Signal flags confirmed, repeated divergence between how work is supposed to happen and how it actually happens.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how you find out your process is being quietly bypassed — before it becomes a compliance problem.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the gap between your designed user flow and what users are actually doing, surfaced automatically.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Requires confidence ≥ Medium per the Confidence Model — below that threshold, it remains a Drift Pattern under observation, not yet a Signal.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain noticing that the official process and what people actually do don't match anymore.

why_it_exists: A single skipped step might be a fluke. Without distinguishing a one-off from a confirmed pattern, the Brain would either cry wolf constantly or miss real structural process gaps.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Not every deviation is a real problem — Drift Signal exists so only confirmed, repeated patterns get escalated, not noise.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this distinction, your product would flag every minor deviation as urgent, drowning out the patterns that actually matter.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: The Drift Candidate → Drift Pattern → Drift Signal staging (Intelligence Architecture Part 10) exists specifically to require repeated, confirmed divergence before escalation — preventing false positives from a single instance.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's not about one person skipping a step once — it's about noticing the same skip happening again and again.

what_it_does: It compares Action Memory (what actually happened) against Rules and SOPs in Factual Memory (what was supposed to happen). A single divergence is a Drift Candidate; a repeated pattern confirmed across multiple instances becomes a Drift Signal — hard evidence of a structural process gap.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It compares what your policy says should happen against what's actually happening, and only escalates once the pattern is confirmed.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the systematic version of 'users keep skipping this step' — backed by evidence, not a hunch.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: Policy → SOP → Workflow comparison. Stages: Drift Candidate → Drift Pattern → Drift Signal (confidence ≥ Medium) → Drift Severity (Low/Medium/High/Critical).
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain catching 'wait, nobody's actually doing it the way the manual says' — and proving it with real evidence.

real_example: Policy requires pricing approval before sending any proposal. Over 90 days, 6 of 18 proposals were sent without recorded approval, confirmed across 3 different account executives. Drift Signal generated: 'Pricing approval step bypassed in 33% of cases. Severity: Medium. Owner: Sales Operations Lead.'
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Detected → Confirmed → Investigated → Resolved. Resolution may occur via Exception (Trust & Governance §3) when the divergence is formally accepted rather than corrected — closing the signal without forcing a process fix.

plain_name: We Don't Know Something We Should
one_sentence: A Knowledge Gap is the Brain recognizing it's missing organizational understanding that creates risk or blocks execution.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the Brain admitting 'we don't actually know this' instead of guessing — and assigning someone to close the gap.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the prompt that tells a user exactly what information is missing before something can move forward.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Actionable by design — identifies a specific gap and assigns explicit responsibility for closing it.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain saying 'nobody's ever actually written this down' — and flagging that as a real problem.

why_it_exists: Reasoning with missing information silently produces bad outcomes. Without surfacing what it doesn't know, the Brain would just guess — or worse, present low-quality conclusions with false confidence.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Decisions made on missing information are quietly worse decisions — this output forces the gap into the open instead of papering over it.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product would either silently fail or guess when key information is missing — neither is acceptable.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Intelligence Architecture's philosophy of explainability (Part 3) requires the Brain to surface uncertainty rather than fabricate it — Knowledge Gap is the structural output for that principle.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain being honest about not knowing something — instead of just making something up.

what_it_does: It searches all memory stores and identifies missing information — an unknown decision-maker, an undocumented process, an unrecorded resolution — then assigns a specific owner and a required action to close the gap within a defined window.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It identifies exactly what's missing and who's responsible for finding the answer, with a deadline.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the structured 'we need this information' prompt your product can route to the right person.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Detected → Investigated → Resolved. Owner example: Domain Expert Group.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It points out a specific blind spot — and tells someone exactly what needs to be figured out, and by when.

real_example: A new enterprise deal reaches contract stage. The Brain finds no procurement contact, no process documentation, and no prior contract history for this client. Knowledge Gap generated: 'Acme Corp procurement process unknown — average contract delay from unknown procurement is 3–5 weeks. Owner: Sarah. Required: establish contact within 5 business days.'
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Detected → Investigated → Resolved. Owner example: Domain Expert Group. Consumed primarily by Consultant (Mission Control surface) per Intelligence Architecture §18's product mapping.

one_sentence: A Prediction is a probabilistic forecast of a future organizational state, based on historical patterns — never presented as certainty.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's a forward-looking forecast grounded in your organization's actual track record, not a generic guess.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the 'here's what's likely to happen' projection that lets a user act before, not after.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Generated from Learning Memory patterns, Action Memory trajectories, and Commitment Memory state — has a full lifecycle, confirmed or falsified as reality unfolds.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's best guess about what's coming next — based on what's happened in similar situations before.

why_it_exists: Without forward projection, the Brain could only ever describe the present and past — never help anyone plan ahead of a likely outcome.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Reacting to what already happened is expensive. Prediction exists so you can act on what's likely to happen instead.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product could only show 'here's the current status', never 'here's where this is heading.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: This is the mechanism behind Simulation Mode's 'Recommended Scenario' output (Intelligence Architecture Part 6) — Prediction is what Simulation reasoning ultimately produces.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain looking at patterns from before and saying 'based on this, here's probably what happens next.'

what_it_does: It forecasts a future state using historical patterns, current trajectory, and active commitments — then tracks the prediction as reality unfolds until it's confirmed or falsified, with either outcome becoming new learning.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It projects where things are trending, grounded in how similar situations actually played out before.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's a forward-looking projection with a confidence level, not a guarantee.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Generated → Tracked → Confirmed / Falsified. Owner: typically the goal or initiative owner the prediction concerns.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a forecast, not a promise — and the Brain keeps tracking it to see if it actually came true.

real_example: Sprint has 9 tasks, 4 closed, 3 days remaining, 2 unresolved blockers. Learning Memory shows similar sprints historically close at 60–68% capacity. Prediction generated: 'Sprint projected to complete at ~65%. Recommended: defer 3 lowest-priority tasks before Friday. Confidence: Medium.'
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Generated → Tracked → Confirmed / Falsified. Drives Simulation Mode's Recommended Scenario output per the Reasoning Pipeline's mode-specific branching (Intelligence Architecture Part 6).

plain_name: Someone Did Something They Shouldn't Have
one_sentence: A Policy Violation is a specific, already-occurred breach of a defined Rule — not a risk of one, and not a pattern of drift.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's a concrete, named instance of a rule being broken — with an owner and a resolution path attached.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the audit flag your product raises the moment a specific compliance rule was actually broken.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Distinct from Operational Risk (future threat) and Drift Signal (repeated pattern) — this is one specific, already-occurred, identifiable breach.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain catching a specific instance of 'this wasn't supposed to happen, but it did.'

why_it_exists: Without distinguishing a specific breach from a risk or a pattern, governance has nothing precise to act on — Policy Violation exists to give a concrete, attributable instance with a clear resolution path.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: A vague sense that 'something might be wrong' isn't actionable for compliance — this output gives a specific, attributable instance instead.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this distinct category, your product couldn't tell the difference between 'might happen' and 'definitely happened.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Governance requires a closeable object with an explicit owner — Policy Violation's lifecycle (Detected → Validated → Escalated → Resolved) is designed for that, unlike Risk or Drift which stay open longer by design.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's not a maybe — it's the Brain saying 'this specific rule was broken, here's the proof.'

what_it_does: It identifies one specific, identifiable instance where a Rule was not followed, assigns it to the Policy owner or relevant authority, and tracks it to formal resolution — either corrected, or closed via an approved Exception acknowledging the deviation.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It names exactly what was broken, by whom, and routes it to the right person to resolve or formally except.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's a specific, auditable compliance flag — not a general warning.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Escalated → Resolved. Owner: typically the Policy owner or relevant Role. Resolution path may be Exception rather than a fix.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain pointing at one specific thing that broke a rule, with proof, so someone can deal with it.

real_example: Policy requires CFO signature on contracts above $100k. A $145,000 contract was executed with only VP Finance signature recorded. Policy Violation generated: 'Contract executed without CFO signature. Owner: CFO Office. Escalated to David Kim for review. Resolution: correct retroactively, or formal Exception.'
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Escalated → Resolved. Closure path may be an Exception (Trust & Governance §3) when the deviation is accepted rather than corrected — Exception is the formal mechanism, not a separate resolution state of the Violation itself.

plain_name: This Step Keeps Slowing Everything Down
one_sentence: A Process Bottleneck is a recurring structural constraint detected from Action Memory — not a one-time delay or someone's bad day.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the structural reason your onboarding (or any process) is consistently slow — pinpointed, not guessed at.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the systemic friction point your analytics would eventually find — except the Brain finds it automatically.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Detected by analyzing Action Memory at scale across many process instances, distinguishing structural delay from case-by-case variance.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain noticing that the exact same step is slow every single time — not just this one time.

why_it_exists: A single slow case might just be unlucky. Without analyzing many instances at scale, nobody could tell a structural bottleneck apart from individual circumstance.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: One slow case is an anecdote. A bottleneck confirmed across 60 cases is a structural problem worth fixing — this output tells you which is which.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, 'this step feels slow' would stay a vague feeling instead of a measured, addressable problem.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Requires aggregate analysis across many instances of the same process type — a single slow case is noise, not signal, for this output type.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain proving that the slowness isn't a one-off — it's the same step, every time.

what_it_does: It analyzes Action Memory across many instances of the same process to find where a specific step consistently exceeds its expected time, regardless of case complexity — pointing to a structural cause like capacity or intake design, not individual performance.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It identifies exactly which step is structurally slow, across the board, and roughly why.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the data-backed version of 'users always get stuck here' — measured, not anecdotal.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Addressed / Accepted. Review Trigger example: Workflow Execution Change.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain pointing at the one step that's consistently the slowest part of a process, every time it runs.

real_example: Across 60 onboarding cases, the legal contract review step takes a median of 11 days against a 3-day target, in 82% of cases, with no relation to case complexity. Process Bottleneck generated: 'Legal review at 3.7x target time in 82% of cases. Root cause: likely capacity or intake. Owner: Legal Team Lead. Priority: High.'
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Detected → Validated → Addressed / Accepted. Review Trigger example: Workflow Execution Change. Consumed by Mission Control's Operational Intelligence surface per Intelligence Architecture §18.

plain_name: Is This AI Agent Ready To Act
one_sentence: Agent Readiness assesses whether an AI agent has enough context and confidence to act autonomously, or must escalate to a human.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the safety check that runs before any AI agent acts on your organization's behalf — confidence first, then action.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why an AI feature sometimes asks a human to confirm instead of just doing the thing automatically.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: One of two required gates before agent action — distinct from Agent Authority (Trust & Governance), which asks if the agent is allowed to act at all.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain double-checking that an AI agent actually knows enough before letting it act on its own.

why_it_exists: Letting an AI agent act without enough context or confidence creates real risk. Without this gate, agents would proceed on assumption instead of waiting for clearance when something important is missing.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Autonomous AI without a readiness check is how AI pilots fail — this is the gate that keeps agents from acting on incomplete information.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, your AI feature might confidently do the wrong thing instead of pausing to ask.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Driven by the same Confidence Model as all other Intelligence Objects (Intelligence Architecture Part 13) — an agent below threshold for a given action escalates rather than acts.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's way of saying 'wait, does this AI actually have enough information before it does this on its own?'

what_it_does: It checks whether an agent has the context, confidence, and clarity required for a specific action class. If everything checks out, the agent is Certified to proceed; if something critical is missing, it reports what's missing and escalates to a human instead of guessing.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It runs a checklist before any agent acts — and if anything's missing, a human gets looped in instead of the agent guessing.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the pass/fail check behind 'agent can proceed automatically' versus 'needs your approval first.'
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Assessed → Certified / Not Ready → Re-Assessed (triggered by new evidence, not time alone). Owner: Agent's supervising Team or Role.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a check the Brain runs to make sure the AI agent isn't missing something important before it acts.

real_example: An agent is tasked with sending a contract renewal. Readiness check: pricing has a recorded Approval, legal review is Completed, contact is verified. Assessment: Certified — proceed. If legal review were missing instead, assessment would be Not Ready — escalate to the Account Executive before sending.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Assessed → Certified / Not Ready → Re-Assessed. Two-axis pairing, not a conflict: Agent Readiness (Intelligence Architecture Part 12, 'can it act confidently?') and Agent Authority (Trust & Governance §9, 'is it allowed to act at all?') — both must pass independently before execution.

one_sentence: Brain Score is an aggregate health metric — confidence, drift severity, and unresolved risk rolled up into one number for a team, project, or org.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's a single, real-time number for how well any team, project, or the whole company is actually performing against its commitments.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the health indicator your product can show at a glance, backed by everything else the Brain already knows.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Not event-driven like other Intelligence Objects — computed by rolling up confidence, drift severity, and unresolved risk across a defined scope.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's like a report card for a team or project — except it updates itself constantly, automatically.

why_it_exists: Without a single rolled-up indicator, understanding organizational health means manually piecing together risks, drift signals, and commitment rates from scratch every time — Brain Score exists so that work is already done.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Before a board call, you shouldn't have to manually assemble the real picture from a dozen different sources — Brain Score is that picture, always current.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without it, your product would need a custom dashboard build for every notion of 'health' instead of one reusable score.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Aggregates across INT-COMP-009 (confidence), Operational Risk severity, and Drift Signal severity — not itself event-driven, but recalculated on material change to any input.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's a quick way to see if a team or project is doing okay — without having to dig through everything yourself.

what_it_does: It rolls up confidence levels, drift severity, unresolved risks, and commitment fulfillment rates into a single score for a defined scope — team, project, business unit, or whole organization — recalculated automatically whenever the underlying reality changes materially.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It's one number that reflects the real operating health of a team or initiative, updated continuously.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's a single composite metric your product can surface as a health badge, trend line, or alert.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Calculated → Published → Recalculated (on material change to inputs). Review Trigger example: Material Change In Inputs.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's like a single grade that tells you how a project is really doing — and it changes automatically as things change.

real_example: Q3 Acme Migration Project Brain Score: 58/100, down from 74 last month — driven by 3 open Operational Risks, 1 active Drift Signal, and a 68% commitment fulfillment rate against an 85% target. Surfaced automatically on the Project Sponsor's morning view. A drop of more than 10 points triggers a Recommendation to initiate a formal review.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Calculated → Published → Recalculated on material change. Surfaced via Ambient Delivery's Executive view per Intelligence Architecture §18's product mapping.

plain_name: Something We Believe To Be True
one_sentence: A Claim is any assertion in the Brain's memory or intelligence, viewed through a trust lens — it carries its own lifecycle of belief.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every fact, decision, and recommendation in the Brain is treated as a claim with a trust status — not just accepted blindly.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why a fact your product shows can carry a visible 'Verified' or 'Challenged' badge instead of just sitting there as plain text.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Not a new stored object — a trust lens applied to existing Memory records and Intelligence Objects, carrying the Trust Lifecycle.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just 'a thing the Brain currently believes' — and like any belief, it can be checked, questioned, or confirmed.

why_it_exists: Treating every assertion as a static, unquestionable fact would make the Brain brittle. Claim exists so every piece of memory or intelligence carries an explicit, evolving trust state instead.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Facts change. Without a trust lifecycle, an outdated fact would sit there as confidently as a verified one — Claim is what prevents that.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product couldn't visually distinguish a freshly-asserted fact from a thoroughly verified one.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without Claim as the unit of trust assessment, there'd be no consistent mechanism to track verification state across Memory and Intelligence uniformly.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why the Brain doesn't treat 'I think this is true' the same as 'this has been checked three times.'

what_it_does: It tracks how trust in an assertion evolves: Asserted → Verified → Trusted → Challenged (if disputed) → Revalidated. Every fact in Factual Memory, every Recommendation, every recorded decision is technically a Claim carrying this lifecycle.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It tracks whether something has just been stated, confirmed, fully trusted, or is currently under dispute.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the underlying state machine behind any 'Verified' or 'Disputed' label your product might show.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle (Trust & Governance v1.0 §13): Asserted → Verified → Trusted → Challenged → Revalidated, bound to the Claim object.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's way of tracking 'how sure are we about this, really?' over time.

real_example: 'Sarah Chen is the primary owner of the Acme Corp account' starts as Asserted. After a manager confirms it, it becomes Verified, then Trusted after months without dispute. When Sarah is promoted and the handover is informal, someone Challenges it — confidence in Acme-related Recommendations drops until a human formally revalidates ownership.
technical_depth: Maps onto existing canonical objects rather than duplicating them (Trust & Governance v1.0 Part 0) — a Claim is a Memory record or Intelligence Object viewed through a trust lens, not a new persisted entity. A Claim re-enters Challenged whenever a Challenge is raised, exiting to Revalidated (rejected) or back to Verified at reduced confidence (accepted, via Memory Model's Conflict Resolution).

one_sentence: Evidence is what makes a Claim trustworthy — the sources and authority that back it up.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's the receipts behind every fact the Brain treats as trustworthy — nothing is taken on faith alone.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the 'source' link a user can click to see exactly where a fact came from.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Not a separate database — it's the existing Sources field on every Memory record and Intelligence Object, now formally governed.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the proof behind a claim — without it, a claim is just someone's assertion.

why_it_exists: A Claim without Evidence is an unverified assertion. Without governing what counts as sufficient backing, the Brain couldn't distinguish a well-supported fact from a guess.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: An unverified assertion treated as fact is how bad decisions get made — Evidence is the check against that.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, every fact your product shows would carry equal weight, whether well-sourced or not.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Defines who may submit Evidence and what authority is required for it to count toward verifying a Claim — without redefining the Sources field itself.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the difference between 'someone said so' and 'here's the document that proves it.'

what_it_does: It governs whether the sources backing a Claim are strong enough to move it from Asserted to Verified to Trusted — weighing authority and independence of sources, not just their existence.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It checks whether a claim is backed by strong, authoritative sources — not just one weak data point.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the data behind a 'view sources' panel for any fact or recommendation.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Depends on Memory Model v1.2's provenance fields and Intelligence Architecture's source fields — this document defines submission authority, not the field itself.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's what actually backs up a claim — and the Brain checks whether that backing is strong enough to really trust it.

real_example: 'Q3 revenue target is $2.4M' is backed by a board-approved plan (CFO source, high authority) and a CRM sales forecast (secondary confirmation). Two independent authoritative sources: Evidence is Strong, and the Claim moves to Trusted. With only the CRM forecast alone, Evidence would be Insufficient — the Claim stays at Asserted.
technical_depth: Owned by Memory Model v1.2 §7 and Intelligence Architecture Part 13 — Trust & Governance does not redefine the Sources/provenance field, only the authority rules for what counts as sufficient Evidence (Part 0 Reconciliation Table).

one_sentence: A Challenge is a formal dispute against a Claim — no fact in the Brain is beyond question.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Anyone with the right standing can formally dispute a fact the Brain holds — nothing is locked in just because it was written down once.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the dispute button a user can click when something the Brain surfaced is actually wrong.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Distinct from Memory Model's automatic Conflict Resolution — Challenge handles human-initiated disputes, not automatically contradicting records.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the formal way to say 'I don't think that's right anymore' — and have it actually get reviewed.

why_it_exists: Organizational truth changes, and authority needs a structured way to revise it. Without Challenge, an outdated or wrong Claim would just sit there with no path to correction.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Locking in facts forever, with no dispute mechanism, guarantees stale information eventually drives bad decisions — Challenge is the safety valve.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, there'd be no structured way for a user to flag 'this is wrong' beyond an email to support.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Requires standing to raise and authority to resolve — distinguishing it from Memory Model's Conflict Resolution, which handles contradicting records automatically rather than human-initiated disputes.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain's way of saying 'you're allowed to push back on this, formally, and someone will actually look at it.'

what_it_does: An authorized Actor disputes a specific Claim. It moves through Raised → Reviewed → Resolved → Accepted/Rejected, with evidence re-examined at each stage and a full audit trail of who challenged, what evidence decided it, and who held resolution authority.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It routes a disputed fact to someone with the authority to resolve it, with a full record of how it was settled.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the workflow behind a 'flag as incorrect' action — review, resolution, audit trail.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Raised → Reviewed → Resolved → Accepted / Rejected. Applies to Memory, Recommendations, Risk Assessments, Agent Actions, and Policy Interpretation.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a formal dispute process — someone raises a concern, someone with authority reviews it, and it gets resolved either way.

real_example: 'Vendor contract renewal date is December 15th' is challenged by Procurement, whose vendor portal shows November 30th. Challenge Raised → Legal Assigned to Review → vendor portal evidence (stronger than the internal calendar reminder) → Challenge Accepted. The original Claim is marked Superseded; the corrected date is Verified.
technical_depth: Division of responsibility (Trust & Governance v1.0 §7): this document defines who has standing to raise a Challenge and under what authority it resolves; Memory Model v1.2 defines how a resolved factual conflict is marked Current/Superseded; Product Architecture defines how it's displayed (Conflict Experience).

one_sentence: An Approval is a formal authorization event — the same governed lifecycle, no matter what context it appears in.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every authorization across the company — memory writes, agent actions, policy exceptions — runs through one consistent, auditable process.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the same 'requires approval' pattern behind every gated action in your product, no matter the feature.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Instantiated differently per context (Write Governance tier, Three-Tier Boundary gate, Adaptive Learning approval) but governed by one shared authority model.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's just 'someone with the right authority signed off on this' — tracked the same way everywhere in the Brain.

why_it_exists: Without one consistent authorization pattern, every gated action in the Brain would need its own bespoke approval logic, making the system inconsistent and harder to audit.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Different approval processes for different things creates audit chaos — Approval exists so it's the same governed pattern everywhere.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without a shared pattern, every gated feature in your product would need its own custom approval logic.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Unifies what would otherwise be separate approval mechanisms across Memory Write Governance, the Three-Tier Boundary, and Adaptive Learning into one lifecycle.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Instead of every kind of approval working differently, it's always the same: requested, reviewed, approved or rejected, then it happens.

what_it_does: It moves through Requested → Reviewed → Approved/Rejected → Executed, regardless of whether it's authorizing a new memory write, an agent action, or a learning update — creating one uniform, auditable record across the whole Brain.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It creates one consistent paper trail for every kind of authorization, anywhere in the system.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the same approval flow your product can reuse for any feature that needs a human sign-off.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Requested → Reviewed → Approved / Rejected → Executed. Instantiated by Write Governance tiers, Three-Tier Boundary gates, and Adaptive Learning approval — same lifecycle, different context.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's always the same four steps: ask, review, decide, then act — no matter what's being approved.

real_example: An AI agent proposes a new learning pattern. Approval lifecycle: Requested (agent submits to governance queue) → Reviewed (Sales Ops Lead examines 14 supporting instances) → Approved → Executed (Memory's Write Governance records the pattern). Full audit trail: who proposed, who approved, when, under what authority.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Requested → Reviewed → Approved / Rejected → Executed (Trust & Governance v1.0 §3). The general pattern this instantiates is the Governance Lifecycle (§6: Proposed → Reviewed → Approved → Executed → Audited) — Memory Writes, Agent Actions, Policy Changes, and Learning Updates are each a specific, simpler case of it.

one_sentence: An Exception is a formally approved deviation from a Rule — the right outcome when a divergence is accepted rather than corrected.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Sometimes breaking a rule is the right call — Exception exists so that's documented and approved, not hidden.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's how your product can show 'this was an approved one-off' instead of just flagging every deviation as a violation.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The formal resolution path for an open Policy Violation or Drift Signal when the divergence is accepted rather than corrected.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's not breaking the rules secretly — it's getting formal permission to deviate, on the record, for a good reason.

why_it_exists: Sometimes following the rule exactly would cause more harm than a controlled, time-bound deviation. Without a formal Exception path, organizations either rigidly enforce rules that don't fit the moment, or quietly break them with no record.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Rigid rule enforcement in every circumstance causes its own damage — Exception lets the organization bend without breaking trust or losing the audit trail.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product would have no way to represent 'this was deliberately and visibly allowed' versus an unnoticed violation.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Closes Policy Violation and Drift Signal objects via acceptance rather than correction — a distinct closure path from 'Resolved-as-fixed'.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's the difference between secretly cutting corners and openly saying 'we're allowing this, just this once, here's why.'

what_it_does: It moves through Proposed → Reviewed → Approved → Active → Expired/Revoked. Once approved, it formally closes the related Policy Violation or Drift Signal, with conditions, a time limit, and automatic restoration of normal enforcement when it expires.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It gives a deviation a clear start, clear conditions, and a clear expiration — after which the rule is back in force automatically.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the time-boxed override behind any 'temporarily allowed' state your product might need to represent.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Proposed → Reviewed → Approved → Active → Expired / Revoked. Closes the related Policy Violation or Drift Signal via acceptance, not correction.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a temporary, approved pass to deviate from the rule — and the rule comes back automatically once it expires.

real_example: A critical bug fix is ready in 2 hours but a full security review takes 48. Exception: Proposed by Engineering Lead → Reviewed by CISO (patch is 3 files, low attack surface) → Approved with conditions → Active. The Policy Violation that would have triggered is closed via Exception, not 'fixed.' It expires automatically at 48 hours, restoring normal enforcement.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Proposed → Reviewed → Approved → Active → Expired / Revoked. Revocation Principle (§5): any Exception may be revoked by an actor with equal or greater authority than the one who granted it — Active → Revoked → Policy Enforcement Restored.

one_sentence: A Delegation transfers existing authority from one Actor to another — it can never create authority that didn't already exist.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It lets authority flex around absences and workload — without ever letting someone grant more power than they actually hold.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's how 'acting on behalf of' actually works under the hood, with a clear paper trail and an expiry date.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Hard constraint: delegated authority may never exceed the authority originally granted — and the chain must remain fully traceable.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's handing your authority to someone else temporarily — but you can't hand over more than you actually have.

why_it_exists: People go on leave, get promoted, or need to redistribute workload — without a formal Delegation mechanism, authority would either freeze up or get exercised informally with no record of who actually approved what.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Without formal delegation, a manager's absence either blocks everything or creates informal, untracked authority — neither is acceptable.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product's 'acting on behalf of' feature would have no real authority model behind it — just a UI label.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: The Delegation Boundary Principle (§5) prevents authority inflation through cascading delegation chains — without it, accountability could quietly dissolve.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's why someone covering for their manager can approve some things, but not suddenly have unlimited power.

what_it_does: It moves through Delegated → Active → Revoked/Expired, with a fully traceable chain of who delegated to whom, when, and under what scope. When it expires or is revoked, authority automatically returns to the original holder.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It tracks exactly who can act on whose authority, for how long, and automatically restores normal authority once it ends.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the time-bound, scoped permission behind any 'covering for' or 'acting on behalf of' state.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Lifecycle: Delegated → Active → Revoked / Expired. Authority automatically returns to the granting actor on expiry or revocation — never silently persists.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a temporary authority handoff — fully tracked, and it automatically goes back to the original person when it's done.

real_example: Maria (VP Sales) delegates her $50k deal approval authority to James while on leave. James can approve deals up to $50k — but not $75k, even with high conviction, because Delegation cannot create authority that didn't exist. When Maria returns and revokes it, James's authority immediately reverts to standard limits.
technical_depth: Lifecycle: Delegated → Active → Revoked / Expired (Trust & Governance v1.0 §3). Delegation Boundary Principle (§5): Rule 1 — delegated authority may never exceed originally granted authority; Rule 2 — delegation chains must remain traceable; Rule 3 — may be constrained by Policy, Ownership, or Three-Tier Boundary.

one_sentence: The Brain surfaces relevant memory inside the tools you already use — Gmail, Slack, Calendar, CRM — without you ever having to search for it.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Your team never has to remember to check a separate app — the right context just shows up where work already happens.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the integration surface: a panel inside Gmail, a suggestion in Slack, a brief before a calendar meeting.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Design Principle: Capture Everywhere, Understand Centrally, Deliver Everywhere. The Brain never interrupts and stays silent when no useful memory exists.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the Brain showing up inside the apps you're already using — you never have to go looking for it separately.

why_it_exists: A destination product that users must remember to open will get forgotten. Without Ambient Delivery, even perfect memory and intelligence would go unused simply because nobody thought to check it.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: The best system in the world is useless if nobody opens it — Ambient Delivery exists so the Brain doesn't depend on anyone remembering to check.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, every insight the Brain generates would require a user to proactively visit a separate dashboard to ever see it.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Directly addresses the v1-to-v2 product shift (Product Architecture §1): from 'open Company Brain, use it, leave it' to 'Company Brain arrives wherever work already is.'
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: If the Brain only lived in its own app, most people would just forget to check it — this is how it avoids that.

what_it_does: It surfaces related commitments, decisions, customer history, and risks directly inside Gmail, Slack, Calendar, and CRM — contextual, dismissible, explainable, and traceable every time, and silent when there's nothing useful to show.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It quietly puts the right context in front of the right person, inside the tool they're already working in.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the Gmail panel, the Slack suggestion, the calendar brief, the CRM context card — all powered by the same underlying memory.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Per-surface behavior: Gmail/Outlook surfaces commitments, decisions, customer history; Slack/Teams surfaces decisions and open commitments; Calendar generates pre-meeting briefs; CRM surfaces relationship history and renewal risk.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's context that just appears, right when you need it, inside the app you're already using — no extra steps.

real_example: Maria opens Gmail to write to the Acme Corp CTO about a contract renewal. Without switching tabs, the Brain surfaces: 3 open commitments linked to this contact, 1 overdue; 2 previous emails about an unresolved pricing concern; a recorded decision approving a custom pricing exception. She has full context before hitting send.
technical_depth: Design Rules (Product Architecture v2.1 §4): the Brain never interrupts, never forces interaction, remains silent when no useful memory exists. Every suggestion is contextual, dismissible, explainable, and traceable. Actions available: Insert Context, View Sources, Ask Consultant, Assign To Agent.

one_sentence: The Brain is an MCP provider — when Claude, ChatGPT, or any AI agent needs organizational context, it asks the Brain instead of guessing.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every AI tool your team uses can be made aware of your company's actual context — instead of confidently making things up.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's why an AI assistant drafting a proposal already knows the client's commitment history, without anyone pasting it in.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Brain acts as MCP provider, not merely consumer. Core tools: brain_search, brain_recall, brain_get_context, brain_get_commitments, brain_get_team_status, brain_check_drift, brain_propose_action.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's how AI tools like Claude or ChatGPT can actually know real things about your company instead of guessing.

why_it_exists: An AI agent without organizational context creates more risk than it eliminates — it will confidently produce generic or wrong output. Without Agent Access, every AI tool your team uses operates blind.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: This is why most AI copilot pilots fail — the AI is smart but blind to your organizational reality. Agent Access is the fix.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, every AI feature you build would need its own bespoke context-fetching logic, repeated per integration.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without a standardized MCP surface, every AI tool integration would require bespoke context injection, breaking the governance and provenance guarantees the rest of the Brain depends on.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Imagine starting a job where nobody tells you anything about the client you're calling — that's an AI agent without Agent Access.

what_it_does: It exposes the Brain's memory and intelligence to any MCP-compatible AI tool — Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Windsurf — so an agent can pull customer history, open commitments, risk flags, and prior context directly, governed by the same trust and provenance rules as human access. It also supports lifecycle context injection (Session Start, Prompt Submit, Task Completion, Turn End) so context isn't forgotten during long-running AI workflows.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It plugs your real organizational knowledge into whatever AI tools your team already uses, safely and with full traceability.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the API surface an AI feature calls to get real context instead of an empty prompt.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: MCP surface: brain_search, brain_recall, brain_get_context, brain_get_commitments, brain_get_team_status, brain_check_drift, brain_propose_action. A2A support allows external agents to request memory, actions, or specialist agents under governance.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's a direct line AI tools can use to ask the Brain real questions about your company, and get real answers back.

real_example: A sales engineer opens Cursor to draft a technical proposal. Without copying anything into the prompt, the Brain provides: the prospect's known technical requirements, a similar proposal that won a comparable deal 6 months ago, and a risk flag that their procurement lead prefers shorter formats. The draft starts from full context, not a blank page.
technical_depth: Core Principle (Product Architecture v2.1 §5): the Company Brain is an MCP provider, not merely a consumer. Also supports Knowledge Exchange — portable knowledge exchange through Canonical Knowledge Objects, OKF-compatible, governed identically to any other organizational action (never bypasses governance).

one_sentence: Mission Control is the dedicated environment for investigation, governance, and oversight — for when ambient context isn't enough.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's where a leader goes to actually investigate something deeply — not the day-to-day surface, but the deep-dive one.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the full workspace view, as opposed to the lightweight inline suggestions Ambient Delivery shows.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Eight surfaces: Personal Reality, Team Reality, Reality Feed, Organizational Memory, Consultant, Operational Intelligence, Drift Experience, Agent System.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the place you go when you need to really dig into something — not just glance at a quick suggestion.

why_it_exists: Some questions need more than a contextual suggestion — investigating a risk, auditing a decision, overseeing agent activity. Without a dedicated deep-dive environment, that kind of work would have nowhere proper to happen.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Before a board call, you need the actual picture, not a glance — Mission Control is built for exactly that kind of deep work.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product would only ever offer shallow, inline suggestions with no way to go deeper when needed.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without a dedicated investigation surface, governance actions (Challenge, Approval review, Agent oversight) would have no proper home distinct from ambient, low-friction suggestions.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Sometimes a quick tip isn't enough — Mission Control is where you go to actually understand what's going on.

what_it_does: It provides eight dedicated surfaces for different kinds of deep work: Personal Reality (what needs my attention), Team Reality (how is my team doing), Reality Feed (what changed), Organizational Memory (why did this happen), Consultant (what should we do), Operational Intelligence (how healthy is the org), Drift Experience, and Agent System.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It gives you eight focused views — from your own priorities to organization-wide health — all backed by the same governed memory.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the full-screen, dedicated views a user navigates to deliberately, as opposed to passive surfacing.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Inputs: all memory types, all intelligence objects, Trust outputs. Mission Control is explicitly not the primary workplace — Ambient Delivery handles day-to-day context; Mission Control is for investigation, governance, coordination, and oversight.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's eight different rooms, each built for a different kind of deep question — like 'what's overdue for me' or 'why did we decide this.'

real_example: The COO wants to understand Q3 initiative health before a board call. She opens Mission Control → Operational Intelligence and sees, in 10 minutes: 6 open Operational Risks across 3 initiatives, 2 active Drift Signals, 12 breached commitments, and a declining Brain Score. She walks into the call with the actual picture, not a status report someone assembled from memory.
technical_depth: Eight Mission Control surfaces (Product Architecture v2.1 §7–14): Personal Reality, Team Reality, Reality Feed, Organizational Memory, Consultant, Agent System, Automation, Operational Intelligence. Organizational Memory includes Inspect Knowledge Object capability for auditing, governance, and AI explainability — not for everyday navigation.

one_sentence: Before the Brain can understand anything, it needs the ten irreducible things every organization is actually made of.

one_sentence_variants.executive: Every decision, project, and workflow your company runs is really just a combination of ten underlying building blocks — this is the Brain's universal language for describing them.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the small, fixed vocabulary the Brain uses to break down literally anything a user does into something structured.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: The foundation layer of the Ontology — Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, State, Time, Relationship. Closed set, fixed since Architecture & Vision v2.2.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's like the alphabet of organizational life — ten basic letters that combine to spell out everything else.

why_it_exists: Earlier drafts tried modeling Entity, Event, Decision, and Context directly — but those turned out to still be composites. Without finding the deepest, non-decomposable primitives, the Brain would be building on an unstable foundation that kept needing redefinition.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: A foundation that keeps shifting underneath you is expensive — these ten primitives were specifically chosen because they don't decompose any further.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without a truly minimal set, every new feature might require inventing a new fundamental concept — these ten are deliberately exhaustive.
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Decision and Workflow are explicitly NOT primitives — they are composites reconstructed from these ten on demand, never stored as independent objects.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: Trying to describe everything with concepts like 'Decision' or 'Project' directly turned out to be too complicated — these ten simpler pieces work better.

what_it_does: It defines Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, State, Time, and Relationship as the foundation every higher-order concept is built from. A Decision, for instance, is just Communication + Goal + Rule + Commitment — never stored as its own thing, always reconstructed from these ten.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It means every complex business concept — a decision, a project, a workflow — can always be traced back to these ten simple parts.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the schema underneath everything: any feature you build ultimately decomposes into these ten types.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Ten primitives, each with a defined Key Question (Who? What was communicated? Who owes what to whom? etc.) per Architecture & Vision v2.2 §5. Everything else in the Ontology — Core Objects, Organizational Structures, Operational Constructs — is built from this layer.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: Once you know these ten things, you can describe basically anything that happens at work.

real_example: A 'Decision' to choose Vendor A over Vendor B isn't a standalone fact stored anywhere — it's reconstructed on demand from the Communication (the discussion), the Goal (cost vs. reliability), the Rule (procurement policy), and the Commitment it created (the signed contract). The same ten pieces describe a hiring decision, a pricing change, or a product launch.
technical_depth: Layer 1 of the four-layer Ontology (Atomic Primitives → Core Objects → Organizational Structures → Operational Constructs), defined jointly in Architecture & Vision v2.2 §5 and Ontology v1.2 §3. Eight of the ten map to Primitive Knowledge Objects (Actor, Communication, Commitment, Action, Resource, Rule, Goal, Relationship); State and Time are cross-cutting attributes with no independent Knowledge Object.

one_sentence: Core Objects are the first-class entities the Brain reasons about — Person, Team, Role, Customer, Vendor, Agent — built from the ten primitives.

one_sentence_variants.executive: It's how the Brain knows the difference between an employee, a customer, a vendor, and an AI agent — each with its own accountability model.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the layer behind every user profile, customer record, or team page your product displays.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Ontology Layer 2 — built from Actor, Relationships, Commitments, and Actions, combined per object type.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the 'who' layer — people, teams, customers, vendors, and AI agents, each properly defined.

why_it_exists: The Atomic Primitive 'Actor' is too abstract to reason about day-to-day — the Brain needs to know the difference between a Person, a Team, and an AI Agent specifically, each with different responsibilities and authority.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Treating every participant identically would erase important distinctions — a customer isn't accountable the same way an employee is. Core Objects exist to capture that.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this, your product couldn't render meaningfully different views for 'a person' versus 'a team' versus 'a customer.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: Without Core Objects, every Composite Knowledge Object downstream (Meeting attendee lists, Commitment owners) would have to work directly with the bare Actor primitive, losing important type distinctions.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's what lets the Brain treat 'a person' differently from 'a whole team' or 'an outside customer.'

what_it_does: It defines Person, Team, Role, Customer, Vendor, and Agent as first-class entities, each built from specific combinations of Actor, Relationships, Commitments, and Actions — with Agent explicitly modeled as an actor in its own right, not merely a tool.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It gives every type of participant in your organization — staff, customers, vendors, AI — its own well-defined identity and accountability.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the typed entity model behind every profile card or directory entry in your product.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Six Core Objects (Ontology v1.2 §3, Layer 2): Person, Team, Role, Customer, Vendor, Agent — each with a 'Built From' composition and standing key questions (e.g. Person: who is this, what do they own, what have they influenced).
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the layer that properly defines 'a person', 'a team', 'a customer', and even 'an AI agent' as distinct, real things.

real_example: Sarah Chen (Person), the Enterprise Sales Team (Team), Acme Corp (Customer), a software vendor (Vendor), and a compliance-checking AI (Agent) are all Core Objects — each built from the Actor primitive but carrying different relationships, commitments, and authority appropriate to what they are.
technical_depth: Ontology Layer 2 (Ontology v1.2 §3). Six objects: Person (Actor, Relationships, Commitments, Actions), Team (Actors, Relationships, Goals, Commitments), Role (Actor, Rule, Commitment, Relationship), Customer (Actor, Goals, Commitments, Actions), Vendor (Actor, Commitments, Resources), Agent (Actor, Rules, Goals, Actions). All map primarily to Factual Memory.

one_sentence: Operational Constructs are the things that represent how work actually happens — Commitment, Task, Workflow, Policy, Decision, Meeting, Incident.

one_sentence_variants.executive: This is the layer that captures the actual operating reality of your company — promises, tasks, policies, and how they really play out.
one_sentence_variants.product: It's the layer behind every task, ticket, meeting, or policy object your product manages.
one_sentence_variants.engineer: Ontology Layer 4 — combines Core Objects and Organizational Structures with Commitment and Action primitives to represent execution-level reality.
one_sentence_variants.new_hire: It's the 'how things actually get done' layer — tasks, policies, meetings, incidents, all properly defined.

why_it_exists: Without a layer specifically for execution-level concepts, there'd be no precise way to distinguish a Policy (what's allowed) from an SOP (how it's supposed to happen) from a Workflow (how it actually happens) — three things that look similar but answer completely different questions.

why_it_exists_variants.executive: Policy, SOP, and Workflow get conflated constantly in most organizations — this layer exists specifically to keep them precisely distinct.
why_it_exists_variants.product: Without this distinction, your product couldn't ever show the gap between 'the documented process' and 'what users actually do.'
why_it_exists_variants.engineer: This is the layer where Drift detection becomes possible — Intelligence compares the SOP (ostensive, designed) against the Workflow (performative, reconstructed from Action Memory) defined here.
why_it_exists_variants.new_hire: It's what lets the Brain tell the difference between 'the rule', 'the plan for following the rule', and 'what people actually do.'

what_it_does: It defines Commitment, Task, Workflow, SOP, Policy, Decision, Meeting, Incident, and Opportunity as Layer 4 objects — most built from Commitment and Action, inheriting the eight-state Commitment lifecycle by default unless explicitly restricted.

what_it_does_variants.executive: It defines every operational concept your company actually runs on — and most of them inherit the same rigorous promise-tracking lifecycle.
what_it_does_variants.product: It's the data model behind tasks, tickets, meetings, and policies in your product, all sharing consistent lifecycle behavior.
what_it_does_variants.engineer: Nine objects (Ontology v1.2 §3, Layer 4): Commitment, Task, Workflow, SOP, Policy, Decision, Meeting, Incident, Opportunity. Workflow and Decision are explicitly not stored — both are reconstructed on demand.
what_it_does_variants.new_hire: It's the layer with all the day-to-day stuff — tasks, meetings, policies, incidents — properly defined so the Brain can track them.

real_example: Policy says client proposals over $100k need VP approval (the constraint). The SOP describes the 8-step process for getting that approval (the design). Workflow is what Action Memory shows actually happened across 60 real proposals (the observation) — and when SOP and Workflow disagree, that's exactly what a Drift Signal catches.
technical_depth: Ontology Layer 4 (Ontology v1.2 §3). Policy vs SOP vs Workflow disambiguation: Policy = the constraint (what's allowed), SOP = the design (how it's supposed to happen, written before execution), Workflow = the observation (how it actually happens, reconstructed from Action Memory). Any object listing Commitment among its Built From components inherits the full 8-state lifecycle by default (Memory Model v1.2 §6.3 defines the only known exceptions).
